subject: literature
notes: Miguel de Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605.
The novel follows an aging gentleman who reads so many tales of chivalry that he sets out to become a knight himself.
In 1614, before Cervantes had finished his own sequel, a writer calling himself Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda published an unauthorized second part.
The true identity of "Avellaneda" remains unknown.
In his own second part, published in 1615, Cervantes has characters mock the false sequel.
He also has Don Quixote change his travel plans in order to avoid the events the false sequel describes.
stem: The student wants to describe the unauthorized sequel and explain how Cervantes responded to it in his own second part. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Cervantes answered Avellaneda's unauthorized 1614 sequel in his own 1615 second part, in which characters mock it and Quixote changes plans to avoid its events.
choices.B: In 1614, before Cervantes finished his own sequel, a writer calling himself Avellaneda, whose true identity is still unknown, published an unauthorized second part.
choices.C: Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote, about a gentleman who reads so many tales of chivalry that he sets out to become a knight, in 1605.
choices.D: In Cervantes's own second part of Don Quixote (1615), characters mock a false sequel, and Don Quixote changes his plans to avoid the events it describes.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: identify the unauthorized sequel (Avellaneda's 1614 second part) and explain Cervantes's response within his own 1615 second part (mockery and a change in Quixote's route). Only one choice does both.
explanation.A: Correct. It identifies the unauthorized sequel and explains both ways Cervantes answered it in his 1615 second part.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It describes the unauthorized sequel but says nothing about how Cervantes responded.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes the first part of the novel, which has nothing to do with the sequel.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes Cervantes's response but refers only vaguely to "a false sequel" without saying who wrote it, when, or that it was unauthorized. This is the most attractive near miss.
